scenes.narration: This scenario involves a vendor needing read-only reports stored in your AWS account. Start at the vendor account on the left. Its own AWS principal calls STS AssumeRole and includes the specified ExternalId, shown as an illustrative acme value. The customer account in the middle owns VendorReadRole. Its trust policy must explicitly identify the vendor principal and require the expected external ID. If the trust checks succeed, STS issues short-lived credentials for that role. Follow the right-hand path to the reports prefix in the customer's S3 bucket. The role should permit only the necessary GetObject access, and an SSE-KMS object may require correctly scoped KMS Decrypt authorization and key policy access. The dashed red path shows a missing or incorrect ExternalId causing the role-assumption request to fail. Across the bottom, the design checklist highlights customer ownership of the role, explicit trust, least-privilege permissions, CloudTrail auditing and revocation. The ExternalId helps prevent the confused-deputy problem; it is not a secret or a standalone authentication credential. The vendor still needs its authorized AWS identity.

scenes.narration: This slide scales the earlier workforce federation pattern to eighty AWS accounts. Start with the enterprise directory on the left. SAML handles employee sign-in, while SCIM handles user and group provisioning into IAM Identity Center. The central service manages identities and access assignments, so you avoid creating separate long-term IAM users in every account. Follow the three illustrated group rows: sandbox admins receive an administrator permission set for sandbox accounts, developers get developer access in nonproduction, and production readers receive read-only permissions in production. A permission set defines the relevant IAM permissions; an assignment connects a user or group, permission set and specific account. Those assignments cause Identity Center to manage IAM roles in target accounts. Along the bottom, employees choose an authorized account through the access portal or CLI single sign-on and receive temporary credentials. The small notes distinguish SCIM from SAML again and remind us that Organizations SCPs can limit access but do not grant it. The correct architecture is centralized workforce SSO with group-based least-privilege assignments, not eighty separate sets of passwords and IAM users.

scenes.narration: This diagram examines two valid approaches to uploading mobile photos into private Amazon S3. The top path starts with a customer signing in through a Cognito user pool. The app receives a signed ID token containing identity claims, but this is not an AWS credential. Next, a Cognito identity pool uses supported authentication to obtain temporary IAM-role credentials. The mobile AWS SDK signs S3 PutObject requests with those temporary credentials, and the bucket policy and IAM role restrict each user to an approved prefix. The lower policy example uses the Cognito identity ID as the prefix variable. Notice the warning: this is different from the user pool's user ID, so using the wrong subject would break isolation. Below, the alternative is a backend-generated presigned upload URL. The mobile client authenticates to the backend, which validates the user and builds a short-lived URL for a specific S3 key and allowed request details. The client uploads without receiving AWS credentials. Compare the decisions along the bottom: identity pools fit direct, limited AWS SDK calls; presigned URLs fit narrowly controlled server-approved uploads. In either design, keep the bucket private and enforce user isolation.

scenes.narration: This example replaces a common risky pattern: embedding permanent IAM access keys in an on-premises batch server. On the left, the scheduled server holds a protected X.509 certificate and private key issued through organizational PKI. Follow the mutual TLS arrow into IAM Roles Anywhere. Inside the service, a trust anchor validates the certificate chain, a profile selects the authorized role, and the role's trust and permissions policies control issuance and use. On the right, the server receives temporary role credentials and performs S3 PutObject only into the nightly-ingest prefix. The four boxes beneath the diagram describe the operating controls: keep your PKI healthy, rotate and revoke certificates, limit the IAM actions and bucket resources, and monitor role assumptions and S3 calls through CloudTrail and other observability. In the comparison card, Roles Anywhere is appropriate when a non-AWS workload can present approved certificates. Federated OIDC is another approach when the workload already has a supported identity token; Systems Manager hybrid activation is for managing machines, not a general API credential broker. The architectural choice is short-lived, traceable access without static keys.
